cost/guess: Softmax turns scores into a guess: one probability for each option. Here, three options get zero point seven, zero point two and zero point one.
cost/loss: Then the right answer is revealed, and we want one number for how bad the guess was. It is called the loss: zero for a perfect guess, and bigger the worse it was.
cost/y: Say the right answer, y, is option zero. The guess gave it zero point seven, a lot, so the loss should be small.
cost/more: Had option two been right, with only zero point one, the loss should be bigger. And a guess sure of a wrong option, giving the truth almost nothing, should cost the most of all.
cost/axes: So draw the loss we want against p y, the probability the guess gave the right answer: no loss at one, and no limit as it falls toward zero.
cost/curve: Minus the natural log, minus ln p, draws exactly that curve.
cost/one: At one, ln one is zero, so a sure, right guess costs nothing. Below one, every log is negative, and the minus sign turns it into a positive cost.
cost/mid: Our guess put zero point seven on the truth. The arrow reads “goes to”: zero point seven goes to a loss of about zero point three six.
cost/low: Put zero point one on it, and the loss is about two point three zero.
cost/zero: As p y falls toward zero, the loss climbs without limit, toward infinity: a sure, wrong guess costs the most.
cost/L: So the loss, L, is minus ln p y: minus the log of the probability on the right answer.
name/surprise: Minus ln p has a simpler reading: surprise. Something you were sure of cannot surprise you, and something you gave only a tenth surprises you a lot.
name/shannon: In 1948, Claude Shannon's paper, A Mathematical Theory of Communication, measured how uncertain a set of probabilities is.
name/entropy: His measure adds up each outcome's surprise, weighted by its own probability: an average surprise. He called it entropy, after the same formula in physics.
name/cross: Cross-entropy crosses two sets of probabilities: the surprise comes from the guess, but the weights come from the truth.
name/only: The truth puts all its weight on the right answer, so only that surprise counts: our loss, minus ln p y.
scores/s: Often you start from the scores instead: two, one and minus one, with option zero right. Softmax adds up e to each score: the total, T, is ten point four eight.
scores/py: The right option's probability is e to its score, over the total: e squared, over T.
scores/quot: The log of a quotient, a top divided by a bottom, is the log of the top minus the log of the bottom.
scores/undo: ln undoes e to a power, so the log of the top, e squared, is just two: the right option's score.
scores/flip: The loss is minus that log, which flips the subtraction: the log of T, about two point three five, minus two, is zero point three five.
scores/rule: Any scores go the same way: the loss is the log of T, minus the right option's score, s y.
uniform/init: When all the scores are equal, every option gets the same share: with C options, one over C. Ten options get a tenth each.
uniform/recip: So the loss is minus ln of a tenth. One over a number flips the sign of its log, so that is ln ten: about two point three zero.
uniform/logC: For any C, equal scores give a loss of ln C, whichever option is right.
uniform/even: That is also Shannon's entropy for an even split, the largest any C outcomes can have: the most uncertain guess there is.
uniform/eight: With eight options, write eight as two cubed, and the power comes out in front: ln eight is three ln two.
uniform/eight2: That is three times zero point six nine three: about two point zero eight.
